```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Shared moon helpers. Phase p: 0 = new, 0.25 = first quarter, 0.5 = full, 0.75 = third quarter.
flSyn = 29.530588853
flPhaseName = p => {
  const age = (((p % 1) + 1) % 1) * flSyn;
  if (age < 1 || age > flSyn - 1) return "New Moon";
  if (Math.abs(age - flSyn / 4) < 1) return "First Quarter";
  if (Math.abs(age - flSyn / 2) < 1) return "Full Moon";
  if (Math.abs(age - 3 * flSyn / 4) < 1) return "Third Quarter";
  const q = age / flSyn;
  return q < 0.25 ? "Waxing Crescent" : q < 0.5 ? "Waxing Gibbous" : q < 0.75 ? "Waning Gibbous" : "Waning Crescent";
}
// Lit part of the Moon as seen from the Northern Hemisphere (waxing = lit on the right)
flMoonPath = (p, r) => {
  p = ((p % 1) + 1) % 1;
  const waxing = p < 0.5;
  const c = Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * p);
  const rx = Math.abs(c) * r;
  const litSweep = waxing ? 1 : 0;
  const termSweep = waxing ? (c < 0 ? 1 : 0) : (c > 0 ? 1 : 0);
  return `M0,${-r} A${r},${r} 0 0 ${litSweep} 0,${r} A${rx},${r} 0 0 ${termSweep} 0,${-r}Z`;
}
flIllum = p => (1 - Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * p)) / 2
flSvg = s => { const d = document.createElement("div"); d.innerHTML = s; return d.firstElementChild; }
flMoonIcon = (p, size = 70) => flSvg(`<svg viewBox="-60 -60 120 120" width="${size}" height="${size}" role="img" aria-label="Moon picture: ${flPhaseName(p)}" style="background:#0b1020;border-radius:50%;max-width:100%"><circle r="50" fill="#334155"/><path d="${flMoonPath(p, 50)}" fill="#f5f0d0"/></svg>`)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
flOrder = (q, n) => {
  let h = 0;
  for (const ch of q) h = (h * 31 + ch.charCodeAt(0)) >>> 0;
  return flD3.shuffler(flD3.randomLcg((h % 10000) / 10000))(flD3.range(n));
}
```

//| echo: false
flBuildCards = function(body, questions, onAnswer) {
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 18px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.1);border:1px solid #e2e8f0;";
    const qp = document.createElement("p");
    qp.style.cssText = "font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;";
    qp.innerHTML = `${qi + 1}. ${qq.q}`;
    card.appendChild(qp);
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.92em;";
    const order = flOrder(qq.q, qq.options.length);
    const shownCorrect = order.indexOf(qq.correct);
    const btns = [];
    order.map(i => qq.options[i]).forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.type = "button";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        btns.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; });
        const right = btns[shownCorrect];
        right.style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; right.style.background = "#f0fff4"; right.style.color = "#22543d"; right.style.fontWeight = "700";
        const ok = oi === shownCorrect;
        if (ok) {
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5"; btn.style.color = "#9b2c2c";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ Not quite. " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
        if (onAnswer) onAnswer(ok);
      };
      btns.push(btn);
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
}
```

// Collapsible inline check: a button that opens a few multiple-choice questions with instant feedback.
flCheck = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="margin:14px 0 24px 0;text-align:center;">
    <button type="button" style="display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;background:linear-gradient(135deg,#4338ca 0%,#0e7490 100%);color:#fff;border:none;padding:10px 22px;min-height:44px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.95em;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;box-shadow:0 3px 12px rgba(67,56,202,.4);">
      <span>📝</span> ${title} <span class="fl-chev" style="transition:transform .3s;">▼</span>
    </button>
    <div style="max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;transition:max-height .5s ease,opacity .4s ease;margin-top:0;text-align:left;"></div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button");
  const chev = outer.querySelector(".fl-chev");
  const body = outer.querySelector("div");
  let open = false;
  toggle.onclick = () => {
    open = !open;
    body.style.maxHeight = open ? "5000px" : "0";
    body.style.opacity = open ? "1" : "0";
    body.style.marginTop = open ? "14px" : "0";
    chev.style.transform = open ? "rotate(180deg)" : "rotate(0)";
  };
  flBuildCards(body, questions);
  return outer;
}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Sorting activity: each statement gets category buttons and instant feedback.
flSorter = function(cats, items, doneMsg) {
  const wrap = html`<div class="fl-card"></div>`;
  const score = html`<div style="font-weight:700;margin-top:8px;"></div>`;
  let right = 0, done = 0;
  items.forEach(it => {
    const row = html`<div class="fl-sortrow"><p>${it.text}</p></div>`;
    const fb = html`<div style="font-size:.9em;"></div>`;
    const btns = cats.map(c => {
      const b = html`<button type="button" class="fl-sortbtn">${c}</button>`;
      b.onclick = () => {
        if (row.dataset.done) return;
        row.dataset.done = "1"; done++;
        const ok = c === it.cat;
        if (ok) right++;
        b.style.borderColor = ok ? "#16a34a" : "#dc2626";
        b.style.background = ok ? "#f0fdf4" : "#fef2f2";
        btns.forEach(x => { if (x.textContent === it.cat) { x.style.borderColor = "#16a34a"; x.style.fontWeight = "700"; } x.style.cursor = "default"; });
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? "✅ " : `❌ It's <b>${it.cat}</b>. `) + it.why;
        fb.style.color = ok ? "#14532d" : "#7f1d1d";
        score.textContent = `${right} of ${done} correct` + (done === items.length ? ` · ${doneMsg}` : "");
      };
      return b;
    });
    btns.forEach(b => row.appendChild(b));
    row.appendChild(fb);
    wrap.appendChild(row);
  });
  wrap.appendChild(score);
  return wrap;
}
```

//| echo: false
// Draft form saved in this browser only (localStorage), with copy and clear buttons.
flForm = function(key, heading, fields) {
  let saved = {};
  try { saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key) || "{}"); } catch (e) { saved = {}; }
  const wrap = html`<div class="fl-card fl-form">${fields.map(([k, lab]) => html`<label class="fl-lbl" for="${key}-${k}">${lab}</label><textarea id="${key}-${k}" data-k="${k}"></textarea>`)}
    <button class="fl-btn" type="button" data-act="copy">📋 Copy my answers</button><button class="fl-btn" type="button" data-act="clear" style="background:#64748b;">Clear</button>
    <span class="fl-status" style="font-size:.85em;" aria-live="polite"></span></div>`;
  const tas = wrap.querySelectorAll("textarea"), status = wrap.querySelector(".fl-status");
  tas.forEach(t => {
    t.value = saved[t.dataset.k] || "";
    t.oninput = () => {
      const o = {}; tas.forEach(x => o[x.dataset.k] = x.value);
      try { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(o)); status.textContent = "Saved in this browser."; } catch (e) { status.textContent = "Couldn't save here; copy your work."; }
    };
  });
  wrap.querySelector("[data-act=copy]").onclick = async () => {
    const text = heading + "\n\n" + fields.map(([k, lab]) => `${lab}\n${wrap.querySelector(`[data-k=${k}]`).value}`).join("\n\n");
    try { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text); status.textContent = "Copied!"; } catch (e) { status.textContent = "Copy failed; select the text and copy it."; }
  };
  wrap.querySelector("[data-act=clear]").onclick = () => {
    tas.forEach(t => t.value = "");
    try { localStorage.removeItem(key); } catch (e) {}
    status.textContent = "Cleared.";
  };
  return wrap;
}

# Engage: Flood Damage {#fl-engage}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🌊 How extreme can flooding be?

In the **Wind 5E** you explained storm winds. In the **Water 5E** you explained rain and snow, and you saw Hurricane Helene flood towns far **inland**. Now we take on the last big piece of storm damage: **flooding at the coast**, when the **ocean** moves onto land.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-facts">
  <div class="fl-fact"><span class="fl-big">14.06 ft</span>Water level at <b>The Battery</b> (the tip of Manhattan) during <b>Hurricane Sandy</b>, 9:24 pm, Oct. 29, 2012. A record. A normal high tide there is about <b>5 ft</b>.</div>
  <div class="fl-fact"><span class="fl-big">7.43 ft</span>Water level at The Battery during <b>Winter Storm Jonas</b>, 8:00 am, Jan. 23, 2016. Jonas was a <i>snowstorm</i>, and it still flooded the coast.</div>
  <div class="fl-fact"><span class="fl-big">🌕 + 🌕</span>Both storms hit New York on the day of a <b>full Moon</b>. Coincidence?</div>
</div>
```

<p style="font-size:.85em;opacity:.9;margin:0;">Water levels are feet above <b>MLLW</b> (mean lower low water), the "0" on tide charts. Source: NOAA Tides &amp; Currents, station 8518750 (The Battery, NY).</p>
:::

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Flood Damage

For each storm (**Winter Storm Jonas**, **Flooding in Marin County**, **Hurricane Sandy**), write:

1. What **initial ideas** do you have about **why this flooding happened**?
2. What initial ideas do you have about **solutions** that could prevent damage like this in the future?

**Brainstorm:** What **factors** do you think contribute to extreme coastal flooding events?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
These are first ideas, so there's no single right answer. Strong answers sound like this:

::: {.fl-table-wrap}
| Storm | Why it flooded (first ideas) | Solutions |
|---|---|---|
| **Jonas** | Strong winds around the storm's low pressure pushed ocean water onto the coast. It hit near **high tide**. | Dunes, sea walls, raising homes and roads, warnings and evacuation |
| **Marin County** | Unusually high **"king tides"** (plus some storm water) pushed the bay onto low roads and homes, several days in a row. | Levees, raising roads, pumps, wetlands that soak up water |
| **Sandy** | Hurricane winds pushed a huge **surge** of water into New York Harbor at **high tide** on a **full Moon**. Water poured into subways and tunnels. | Flood gates, covers for subway entrances, sea walls, raising equipment |
:::

**Brainstorm factors:** strong onshore wind, low air pressure, **high tide**, **full or new Moon**, rain and runoff, **sea-level rise**, low-lying land, the shape of the coast or harbor, the storm's timing.
:::

# Explore 1: Moon Phases and Eclipses Investigation {#fl-explore1}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🔦 How do moon phases and eclipses occur?

In class you build a model of the **Sun-Earth-Moon system** in a dark room:

- one student holds a **flashlight** (the **Sun**),
- one student holds a **ball on a stick** (the **Moon**); that student's **head is Earth**,
- everyone else moves around to watch from **outside** the system.

Your job: arrange the model to match **8 pictures of the Moon**, and look for **patterns**. The explanation comes later.
:::

## The ball-and-flashlight model {#fl-model}

No dark room at home? Use this virtual version. The big panel is the view **from above** (not to scale), with the flashlight Sun on the **right**, like the diagram in your packet. Below it are **three observers**: the person who is Earth, the person holding the flashlight, and an outside observer.

**Tip from the investigation scaffold:** hold the ball **a little above eye level** for phases, so your head doesn't block the light. For eclipses (questions 7–8), move it to **exactly eye level**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
flPlayBtn = {
  const b = html`<button type="button" class="fl-btn">▶ Play one lunar month</button>`;
  b.onclick = () => {
    const input = viewof flDay;
    let t = 0;
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      t = Math.round((t + 0.25) * 100) / 100;
      input.value = Math.min(t, 29.5);
      input.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
      if (t >= 29.5) clearInterval(timer);
    }, 70);
  };
  return b;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const p = flDay / flSyn;
  const W = 420, H = 300, cx = 175, cy = 150, R = 110, rm = 14, re = 26;
  const phi = 2 * Math.PI * p;                       // 0 = toward the Sun (right), counterclockwise
  const mx = cx + R * Math.cos(phi), my = cy - R * Math.sin(phi);
  const ang = ((phi * 180 / Math.PI) % 360 + 360) % 360;
  const nearNew = ang < 6 || ang > 354, nearFull = Math.abs(ang - 180) < 6;
  const solar = flEyeLevel && nearNew, lunar = flEyeLevel && nearFull;
  let s = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" role="img" aria-label="Top view of the model: flashlight Sun on the right, Earth in the middle, Moon at ${Math.round(ang)} degrees around its orbit" style="width:100%;background:#0b1020;border-radius:12px;font:12px sans-serif">`;
  s += `<defs><marker id="flArr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="5" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0L10,5L0,10z" fill="#fde68a"/></marker></defs>`;
  for (let k = 0; k < 6; k++) { const y = 30 + k * 48; s += `<line x1="${W - 8}" y1="${y}" x2="${W - 70}" y2="${y}" stroke="#fde68a" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#flArr)" opacity=".8"/>`; }
  s += `<text x="${W - 8}" y="16" fill="#fde68a" font-weight="700" text-anchor="end">Sunlight (flashlight) ☀️</text>`;
  if (flEyeLevel) s += `<polygon points="${cx},${cy - re} 0,${cy - re + 8} 0,${cy + re - 8} ${cx},${cy + re}" fill="#000" opacity=".55"/><text x="6" y="${cy + re + 4}" fill="#94a3b8">Earth's shadow</text>`;
  s += `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${R}" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>`;
  s += `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${re}" fill="#1e3a8a"/><path d="M${cx},${cy - re} A${re},${re} 0 0 1 ${cx},${cy + re}Z" fill="#60a5fa"/>`;
  s += `<text x="${cx}" y="${cy + re + 15}" fill="#cbd5e1" text-anchor="middle">Earth (your head)</text>`;
  s += `<circle cx="${mx}" cy="${my}" r="${rm}" fill="${lunar ? "#7c2d12" : "#334155"}"/>`;
  if (!lunar) s += `<path d="M${mx},${my - rm} A${rm},${rm} 0 0 1 ${mx},${my + rm}Z" fill="#f5f0d0"/>`;
  s += `<line x1="${cx}" y1="${cy}" x2="${mx}" y2="${my}" stroke="#a5b4fc" stroke-dasharray="2 3" opacity=".7"/>`;
  s += `<text x="8" y="${H - 8}" fill="#94a3b8">Moon orbits counterclockwise (seen from above the North Pole)</text>`;
  s += `</svg>`;
  const view = (inner, label) => html`<div style="flex:1 1 110px;min-width:0;text-align:center;font-size:.85em;">${flSvg(`<svg viewBox="-60 -60 120 120" role="img" aria-label="${label}" style="width:110px;height:110px;max-width:100%;background:#0b1020;border-radius:50%">${inner}</svg>`)}<div><b>${label}</b></div></div>`;
  const earthInner = solar ? `<circle r="56" fill="#fde68a" opacity=".35"/><circle r="50" fill="#020617"/>`
                   : lunar ? `<circle r="50" fill="#9a3412"/>`
                   : `<circle r="50" fill="#334155"/><path d="${flMoonPath(p, 50)}" fill="#f5f0d0"/>`;
  const sunInner = nearFull && flEyeLevel ? `<circle r="50" fill="#1e3a8a"/><text y="5" fill="#cbd5e1" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">Earth blocks it</text>`
                 : `<circle r="50" fill="#f5f0d0"/>`;
  const outInner = `<circle r="50" fill="#334155"/><path d="M0,-50 A50,50 0 0 1 0,50Z" fill="#f5f0d0"/>`;
  const msg = solar ? "🌑 <b>Solar eclipse set-up:</b> the ball (Moon) blocks the flashlight (Sun) from Earth's eyes. Its shadow falls on your face. (Question 7)"
            : lunar ? "🌕 <b>Lunar eclipse set-up:</b> your head (Earth) blocks the light from reaching the ball (Moon). (Question 8)"
            : flEyeLevel ? "At eye level, an eclipse only happens when the three line up exactly. Slide to day 0 or about day 14.8."
            : `Phase seen from Earth: <b>${flPhaseName(p)}</b> · ${Math.round(flIllum(p) * 100)}% of the face we see is lit.`;
  return html`<div class="fl-svg-wrap">${flSvg(s)}
    <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:10px;margin-top:10px;">

## 🔑 Check your diagrams (try it first!)
The packet's pictures may be in a different order. Match each picture by its **shape**. Each diagram should show the flashlight, the head (Earth), the ball (Moon), the **lit half of the ball facing the flashlight**, and a sight line from the head to the ball.

::: {.fl-table-wrap}
| Moon picture | Where the ball is (seen from above) |
|---|---|
| **New** (dark) | Between the flashlight and your head. You see the unlit side. |
| **Waxing crescent** (thin sliver lit on the right) | Turn left (counterclockwise) about 45° from the flashlight. |
| **First quarter** (right half lit) | 90° from the flashlight. |
| **Waxing gibbous** | About 135° around. |
| **Full** | Opposite the flashlight, behind your head, held a little **above** your head's shadow. |
| **Waning gibbous** | About 225° around. |
| **Third quarter** (left half lit) | About 270°: 90° from the flashlight on the other side. |
| **Waning crescent** (sliver lit on the left) | About 315°, almost back to the flashlight. |
:::

Turning **counterclockwise** (to your left) gives the order people in New York see: lit on the **right** while waxing.
:::

## How long is the cycle? {#fl-calendar}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 📌 A note about your packet: "Look at the moon calendar again"
Question 6 says to look at the moon calendar "again," but the SY 26-27 packet doesn't have a moon calendar anymore. (It was part of an older version of this lesson.) Use the calendar below instead.
:::

Each circle is the Moon's shape on one day (**calculated** from the average lunar month, not photos, so a phase can be off by up to about a day). **Tap any Moon** to see its date and phase. Red rings mark Hurricane Sandy (Oct. 29, 2012) and Winter Storm Jonas (Jan. 23, 2016).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flYear = Inputs.number([1900, 2100], {label: "Year", value: 2025, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const refNew = Date.UTC(2000, 0, 6, 18, 14);
  const phaseOf = t => { const days = (t - refNew) / 86400000; return (((days / flSyn) % 1) + 1) % 1; };
  const cell = 22, r = 8.5, left = 40, top = 24;
  const W = left + 31 * cell + 6, H = top + 12 * cell + 6;
  const monthFmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {month: "short", timeZone: "UTC"});
  const events = {"2012-9-29": "Hurricane Sandy hit NYC", "2016-0-23": "Winter Storm Jonas hit NYC"};
  const readout = html`<div style="min-height:2.6em;font-size:.95em;margin:6px 0;padding:8px 12px;border-radius:10px;background:#1e1b4b;color:#e0e7ff;">👆 Tap a Moon to see its date and phase.</div>`;
  const svg = flD3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("role", "img")
    .attr("aria-label", `Moon phase calendar for ${flYear}: one row per month, one calculated moon shape per day`)
    .style("width", "100%").style("height", "auto").style("background", "#0b1020")
    .style("border-radius", "12px").style("font", "10px sans-serif");
  for (let d = 1; d <= 31; d++)
    svg.append("text").attr("x", left + (d - 0.5) * cell).attr("y", top - 9).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("fill", "#94a3b8").text(d % 5 === 0 || d === 1 ? d : "");
  for (let m = 0; m < 12; m++) {
    const y = top + (m + 0.5) * cell;
    svg.append("text").attr("x", 6).attr("y", y + 3.5).attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").text(monthFmt.format(new Date(Date.UTC(flYear, m, 1))));
    const nDays = new Date(Date.UTC(flYear, m + 1, 0)).getUTCDate();
    for (let d = 1; d <= nDays; d++) {
      const t = Date.UTC(flYear, m, d, 12);
      const p = phaseOf(t);
      const ev = events[`${flYear}-${m}-${d}`];
      const g = svg.append("g").attr("transform", `translate(${left + (d - 0.5) * cell},${y})`).style("cursor", "pointer");
      g.append("circle").attr("r", r + 2).attr("fill", "transparent");
      g.append("circle").attr("r", r).attr("fill", "#334155");
      g.append("path").attr("d", flMoonPath(p, r)).attr("fill", "#f5f0d0");
      const label = `${new Date(t).toLocaleDateString("en-US", {timeZone: "UTC", dateStyle: "medium"})}: ${flPhaseName(p)} (about ${Math.round(flIllum(p) * 100)}% lit)`;
      g.append("title").text(label);
      g.on("click", () => { readout.textContent = "🌙 " + label + (ev ? ` · ${ev}!` : ""); });
      if (ev) g.append("circle").attr("r", r + 2.5).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#f87171").attr("stroke-width", 2.2);
    }
  }
  return html`<div>${svg.node()}${readout}</div>`;
}
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: questions 5–6

5. How must the Moon **move** in order for the pattern to repeat itself?
6. Look at the moon calendar. How **long** does it take for the pattern to start repeating itself?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
5. The Moon must **orbit (revolve) all the way around Earth**, counterclockwise as seen from above the North Pole, until it's back in the **same position compared to the Sun and Earth**.
6. About **29.5 days** (29.53), from one full Moon to the next. That's about a month.

**Why not 28 days?** You might hear "28 days" (even some teacher materials say it). The Moon goes once around Earth **compared to the stars** in about **27.3 days**. But Earth is moving around the Sun at the same time, so the Moon needs about **2 more days** to line up with the Sun again. Phases depend on the Sun, so the phase cycle is **29.5 days**. (Source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet.)
:::

Turn on **eclipse mode** in the model above, then slide to day **0** and to about day **14.8**.

### ✏️ In your packet: questions 7–8

7. Find a set of positions where the **"Moon" fully blocks the light of the "Sun"** from the perspective of "Earth." **Draw** it.
8. Find a set of positions where **"Earth" fully blocks the light of the "Sun"** from reaching the "Moon." **Draw** it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
7. Flashlight, ball, and head in **one straight line at eye level**, with the **ball between** the flashlight and your head. The ball's shadow falls on your face. That's a **solar eclipse**, and it can only happen at **new Moon**.
8. Flashlight, head, and ball in **one straight line at eye level**, with the ball **behind your head**. Your head's shadow covers the ball. That's a **lunar eclipse**, and it can only happen at **full Moon**.

**Key insight:** when the ball is held **above** eye level, the same positions just give a new Moon and a full Moon, with **no** eclipse. Height (up or down) matters!
:::

## Making Sense of the Investigation {#fl-making-sense1}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Making Sense of the Moon Phases and Eclipses Investigation

**See-Think-Wonder**

- **See:** What did the person who was **Earth** observe? The person who was the **Sun**? The **observers outside** the system?
- **Think:** Why do you think these observers saw different things?
- **Wonder:** What questions do you have?

**Analysis 1.** Based on the model, explain **what causes the appearance of moon phases** on Earth.

In class this is shared with **Domino Discover**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

::: {.fl-table-wrap}
| Observer | See | Think |
|---|---|---|
| **Earth** (the head) | Different amounts of the lit ball as it moved: dark, sliver, half, mostly, full, and back. | What we see depends on **where the Moon is** compared to us and the Sun. |
| **Sun** (flashlight) | Always the **fully lit** side of the ball (except when the head blocked it). | The Sun always lights half the Moon. The Sun never "sees" phases. |
| **Outside observers** | The ball was always **half lit, half dark**, and the lit half always faced the flashlight. | Phases are about **viewpoint**. Someone outside the system wouldn't see phases. |
:::

**Wonder (examples):** Why don't we get an eclipse every month? Why do we always see the same side of the Moon? Does everyone on Earth see the same phase?

**Analysis 1:** The **Sun always lights half the Moon**. As the Moon **orbits** Earth, its **position** compared to the Sun and Earth changes, so we see **different amounts of the lit half**. New Moon: the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so we see its dark side. Full Moon: Earth is between, so we see the whole lit side. Phases are **not** caused by Earth's shadow.
:::

   correct: 1,
   explanation: "That's the model's version of the real Moon's tilted orbit, which you'll see in Explain 1."}

# Explain 1: Explaining Lunar Patterns {#fl-explain1}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🧠 How do positions cause phases and eclipses?

Now you'll turn the patterns from your model into an explanation, using the **Moon Phases Simulator** and an eclipse model. Your explanation should use the **relative positions** of the Moon, Earth, and Sun, and the **perspective of the observer**.
:::

## Part 1: Moon phases {#fl-phases}

### ✏️ In your packet: Part 1. Moon Phases, steps 1–3

1. Open the **Moon Phases Simulator**.
2. Switch to the **"Horizon Diagram"** tab. It shows how the Moon's movement around Earth causes different phases, and where the Moon is in the sky during the day.
3. **Click and drag** the Moon around Earth. Watch how the phase and the Moon's position on the horizon change.

### ✏️ In your packet: questions 4–5

4. If you could view the Moon from the **Sun's** point of view, how much of the Moon would be **illuminated** at each position?
5. Why does the amount of the Moon that's illuminated look **different from Earth**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
4. **All** of the side facing the Sun. From the Sun, the Moon would look **fully lit at every position**. (Half of the whole Moon is always lit.)
5. From Earth we look at the Moon from a **different angle** at each position in its orbit, so a different part of the lit half **faces us**.
:::

### Predict the phase from the position (questions 6–7)

Here is a top view like the one in your packet, with **sunlight coming from the right**. The Moon is shown at **8 numbered positions**. Use it for **question 6** (what does the Moon look like from Earth at positions 1, 2, 3, and 6?) and **question 7** (which position matches each picture?).

**Tip:** imagine standing on Earth and facing the Moon. How much of its **lit (right) half** faces you?

```{ojs}

Position 1 is between Earth and the Sun, and the numbers go counterclockwise." style="width:100%;max-width:520px;background:#0b1020;border-radius:12px;font:12px sans-serif">`;

{
  const names = ["New Moon", "Waxing Crescent", "First Quarter", "Waxing Gibbous", "Full Moon", "Waning Gibbous", "Third Quarter", "Waning Crescent"];
  const sorted = names.slice().sort();
  const q6 = [1, 2, 3, 6].map(pos => {
    const sel = html`<select aria-label="Phase seen from Earth at position ${pos}" style="min-height:44px;font-size:.95em;max-width:100%;"><option value="">Choose...</option>${sorted.map(o => html`<option>${o}</option>`)}</select>`;
    const mark = html`<span style="margin-left:6px;font-weight:700;"></span>`;
    return {pos, sel, mark, ok: () => sel.value === names[pos - 1],
      row: html`<div style="display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;margin:4px 0;flex-wrap:wrap;"><b style="background:#6366f1;color:#fff;border-radius:50%;width:28px;height:28px;display:inline-flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;">${pos}</b>${sel}${mark}</div>`};
  });
  const pics = [{p: 0.5, ans: 5}, {p: 0.875, ans: 8}, {p: 0.375, ans: 4}, {p: 0.75, ans: 7}];
  const q7 = pics.map((pc, i) => {
    const sel = html`<select aria-label="Position number for picture ${i + 1}" style="min-height:44px;font-size:.95em;"><option value="">Position?</option>${[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].map(n => html`<option>${n}</option>`)}</select>`;
    const mark = html`<div style="font-weight:700;min-height:1.4em;"></div>`;
    return {sel, mark, ok: () => +sel.value === pc.ans, cell: html`<div>${flMoonIcon(pc.p, 70)}<div>${sel}</div>${mark}</div>`};
  });
  const msg = html`<div style="margin-top:8px;font-size:.95em;"></div>`;
  const btn = html`<button type="button" class="fl-btn">Check my answers</button>`;
  btn.onclick = () => {
    let n = 0;
    q6.forEach(r => { const ok = r.ok(); if (ok) n++; r.mark.textContent = r.sel.value ? (ok ? "✅" : "❌") : ""; });
    q7.forEach(r => { const ok = r.ok(); if (ok) n++; r.mark.textContent = r.sel.value ? (ok ? "✅" : "❌") : ""; });
    msg.innerHTML = n === 8 ? "🎉 <b>8 / 8!</b> Position 1 is between Earth and the Sun (new). Position 5 is opposite the Sun (full). The Sun lights the right half of the Moon at every position."
      : `<b>${n} / 8 correct.</b> Hint: positions go counterclockwise from the Sun's side. The lit part grows on the right first (waxing), then shrinks from the right (waning).`;
  };
  return html`<div class="fl-card">
    <p style="margin:0 0 6px;"><b>Question 6.</b> What does the Moon look like from Earth at each position?</p>
    ${q6.map(r => r.row)}
    <p style="margin:14px 0 6px;"><b>Question 7.</b> Write the position number under each picture.</p>
    <div class="fl-moonpick">${q7.map(r => r.cell)}</div>
    ${btn}${msg}</div>`;
}
```

In some copies of the packet, the questions in Part 1 are numbered 1–6 and then **restart at 4 and 5**. This chapter calls those last two **question 7** (write the position numbers) and **question 8** (explain to your friends).

### ✏️ In your packet: question 8

You're out at night with friends. One points out that the Moon is **full**, and everyone starts wondering why the Moon looks different on different nights. **Explain the pattern** to your friends. Use all of these words: **Moon, Sun, Earth, sunlight, orbit, position, visible, illuminated**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
"The **Moon** doesn't make its own light. **Sunlight** from the **Sun** always **illuminates** half of it. The Moon **orbits** **Earth** about every 29.5 days, so its **position** keeps changing. Tonight it's on the far side of Earth from the Sun, so the whole lit half is **visible** to us: a full Moon. In about a week it will be off to the side, and we'll see only half of the lit part. In about two weeks it will be between us and the Sun, and the lit side will face away from us (new Moon)."
:::

## Eclipses {#fl-eclipses}

Usually, when the Moon orbits Earth, it is **not** in a perfect line with the Sun. The Moon may be on the same side of Earth as the Sun, or on the opposite side, but usually not in a straight line. In class your teacher demonstrates this with the ball and flashlight, and shows the **Eclipse Explorer** ("Earth-Moon Side View").

<a class="fl-sim-link" href="https://astro.unl.edu/smartphone/EclipseExplorer/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">🌒 Open the Eclipse Explorer (University of Nebraska–Lincoln)</a>

Here's a side view to try. The Moon's orbit is **tilted about 5°** compared to Earth's path around the Sun (drawn much bigger here so you can see it). Change how long it's been since an **eclipse season**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flEclPhase = Inputs.radio(["New Moon", "Full Moon"], {value: "New Moon", label: "Phase:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flEclMonths = Inputs.range([0, 12], {step: 0.5, value: 0, label: "Months since an eclipse season:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  // Model: the Sun's angle from the line where the two orbits cross advances 360° per eclipse year (346.62 days)
  const lam = 2 * Math.PI * (flEclMonths * flSyn) / 346.62;
  const beta = 5.14 * Math.sin(lam);
  const solar = flEclPhase === "New Moon";
  const limit = solar ? 1.5 : 1.0;
  const ecl = Math.abs(beta) < limit;
  const W = 420, H = 220, cy = 110, mx = solar ? 210 : 330;
  const earthX = solar ? 330 : 210;
  const dy = -beta * 14;
  let s = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" role="img" aria-label="Side view: Sun on the left, Earth and Moon on the right. The Moon sits ${beta.toFixed(1)} degrees ${beta >= 0 ? "above" : "below"} the plane of Earth's orbit. ${ecl ? "Eclipse." : "No eclipse."}" style="width:100%;background:#0b1020;border-radius:12px;font:12px sans-serif">`;
  s += `<circle cx="20" cy="${cy}" r="40" fill="#fbbf24"/><text x="20" y="${cy + 58}" fill="#fde68a" text-anchor="middle">Sun</text>`;
  s += `<line x1="0" y1="${cy}" x2="${W}" y2="${cy}" stroke="#475569" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>`;
  s += `<text x="66" y="${cy + 16}" fill="#94a3b8">plane of Earth's orbit</text>`;
  if (solar) {
    s += `<polygon points="${mx},${cy + dy - 9} ${W},${cy + dy - 3} ${W},${cy + dy + 3} ${mx},${cy + dy + 9}" fill="#000" opacity=".6"/>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${earthX}" cy="${cy}" r="24" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="${earthX}" y="${cy + 42}" fill="#cbd5e1" text-anchor="middle">Earth</text>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${mx}" cy="${cy + dy}" r="9" fill="#e2e8f0"/><text x="${mx}" y="${cy + dy - 14}" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">Moon</text>`;
  } else {
    s += `<polygon points="${earthX},${cy - 24} ${W},${cy - 14} ${W},${cy + 14} ${earthX},${cy + 24}" fill="#000" opacity=".6"/>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${earthX}" cy="${cy}" r="24" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="${earthX}" y="${cy + 42}" fill="#cbd5e1" text-anchor="middle">Earth</text>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${mx}" cy="${cy + dy}" r="9" fill="${ecl ? "#b45309" : "#e2e8f0"}"/><text x="${mx}" y="${cy + dy - 14}" fill="#e2e8f0" text-anchor="middle">Moon</text>`;
  }
  s += `</svg>`;
  const result = ecl ? (solar ? "🌑 Solar eclipse! The Moon's shadow reaches Earth." : "🌕 Lunar eclipse! The Moon passes through Earth's shadow.")
                     : (solar ? "No eclipse: the Moon's shadow passes above or below Earth." : "No eclipse: the full Moon passes above or below Earth's shadow.");
  return html`<div class="fl-svg-wrap">${flSvg(s)}
  <div class="fl-cards">
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Moon above (+) or below (−) Earth's orbital plane</span><b class="fl-big">${beta >= 0 ? "+" : ""}${beta.toFixed(1)}°</b>(max about ±5°)</div>
    <div class="fl-stat" style="flex:2 1 220px;"><span class="fl-lab">Result</span><b class="fl-big" style="font-size:1.1em;color:${ecl ? "#b91c1c" : "#0f172a"}">${result}</b></div>
  </div>
  <p class="fl-note">Simplified model. Eclipse if the Moon is within about 1.5° (solar) or 1.0° (lunar) of the plane. Tilt drawn about 14 times too big.</p></div>`;
}
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: How does the path of the Moon around Earth change?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
The Moon's orbit is **tilted about 5°** compared to Earth's path around the Sun, so at most new and full Moons the Moon is **above or below** the Sun-Earth line. The tilted orbit doesn't go flat. Instead, the two places where it **crosses** Earth's orbital plane slowly line up with the Sun about **twice a year** (two **eclipse seasons**, about 6 months apart). Only then can a new or full Moon make an eclipse.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 📌 A note about your packet's wording
The packet says that sometimes the Moon's "path becomes aligned with the path of the Earth around the sun." The tilt actually stays about **5°** all the time. What changes is **where the Moon is** when it crosses Earth's orbital plane. An eclipse happens only when a new or full Moon falls **near one of those two crossing points**.
:::

In class you watch this video and **annotate the two Eclipse Models** in your packet. Your teacher plays **0:00–3:16, 4:14–5:09, and 6:45–8:25**.

```

### ✏️ In your packet: annotate the Eclipse Models

Label each model with:

- **which eclipse** is which,
- the **sizes** of the Moon and the Sun compared,
- the **distances** from Earth to the Moon and from Earth to the Sun compared,
- how the **viewer's location** on Earth changes what they see.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your annotations (try it first!)

::: {.fl-table-wrap}
| | Solar eclipse | Lunar eclipse |
|---|---|---|
| **Line-up** | Sun → **Moon** → Earth (**new Moon**) | Sun → **Earth** → Moon (**full Moon**) |
| **Whose shadow?** | The **Moon's** shadow falls on Earth | **Earth's** shadow falls on the Moon |
| **Sizes and distances** | The Sun is about **400 times wider** than the Moon but about **400 times farther** away, so they look about the same size from Earth and the Moon can just cover the Sun | Earth's shadow is much bigger than the Moon, so it can cover the whole Moon, which often turns **red-orange** |
| **Who sees it** | Only people in the Moon's dark shadow see a **total** eclipse (a narrow path); people nearby see a partial one | **Anyone on Earth's night side** (where the Moon is up) sees it at the same moment |
:::
:::

## Think-Talk-Open Exchange {#fl-ttoe}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Think-Talk-Open Exchange

Use a **model and words** for each:

1. How are the conditions that create **new Moons** similar to and different from **solar eclipses**? Include the role of the **monthly** and **longer (annual)** time scales, and the **perspective of the observer**.
2. How are the conditions that create **full Moons** similar to and different from **lunar eclipses**? Include the same two ideas.

**Reflection:** What are some new ideas you heard in your group discussion?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
1. **Similar:** both happen when the Moon is **between Earth and the Sun**. **Different:** a new Moon happens **every 29.5 days** because the Moon only has to be *roughly* between. A solar eclipse needs an **exact line**, which only happens during eclipse seasons, a few times a year at most. **Observer:** everyone has the new Moon on the same date, but only people in the Moon's shadow path see the eclipse (total in a narrow strip).
2. **Similar:** both happen when **Earth is between** the Sun and the Moon. **Different:** full Moon every 29.5 days; a lunar eclipse only when they line up exactly, so it's rarer. **Observer:** anyone on Earth's **night side** sees the full Moon and the eclipse at the same moment (at different clock times in different time zones).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 📌 Two things people often get wrong
- **"Everyone on Earth can see a lunar eclipse."** Only people on Earth's **night side**, where the Moon is above the horizon, can see it.
- **"Everyone sees the new Moon at night."** A new Moon is on the **Sun's side** of Earth, so it's up in the **daytime** and rises and sets with the Sun. You can't see it at all. The **full** Moon is the one that's up all night.
:::

::: {.key-idea}
### 🔑 Class consensus: phases and eclipses
- The Sun always lights **half** the Moon. The Moon's **position in its orbit** decides how much of that lit half we see. That's the **phase**. It is **not** Earth's shadow.
- Phases repeat every **29.5 days**. Everyone on Earth sees the same phase on the same day.
- **Solar eclipse** = new Moon in an **exact** line; seen only from the Moon's shadow path. **Lunar eclipse** = full Moon in an exact line; seen from Earth's whole night side.
- Eclipses are rarer because the Moon's orbit is **tilted about 5°**; they cluster in eclipse seasons about 6 months apart.
- Open question: **How do moon phases relate to tides and flooding?**
:::

# Explore 2: High Tides and Moon Phases {#fl-explore2}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🌊 How are the Moon and tides related?

Our class pivoted to the Moon because many of us thought **moon phases affect tides**, and **tides affect flooding**. Now you'll test that with real data. You'll graph tides at **The Battery** in New York City at **three time scales**: one **day**, one **month**, and one **year**. Look for patterns. The explanation comes in Explain 2.
:::

**High tide** is when the sea reaches its highest level on the shore; **low tide** is its lowest. In class you look at pictures of the same shore at high and low tide. The difference in height between them is the **tidal range**.

## The data: Tidal Fluctuation Data {#fl-tide-data}

Your teacher gives you a handout called **Tidal Fluctuation Data** (its file may be titled *Highest and Lowest Tides by Month*). It has three tables, all for **The Battery, NY** (NOAA station 8518750), in **feet above MLLW**, local time. These are **predicted** tides: they come from the positions of the Moon and Sun only, with **no weather** in them. That's what makes them useful for testing the Moon idea.

## 📌 Notes about the data handout
- **The Moon Phase column in the January table is blank** in the handout, but you need it to match tides to phases. We filled it in above: **new Dec. 30 · first quarter Jan. 6 · full Jan. 13 · third quarter Jan. 21 · new Jan. 29** (dates calculated for Eastern time).
- **Blank cells (Jan. 5, 11, 19, 26) are real, not missing data.** Each tide comes about **50 minutes later** than the day before, so sometimes a high or low slides past noon or midnight and that half of the day has only one. **Skip** those cells. Don't plot them as zero.
- **The yearly table lists tides on the phase date.** The biggest tides often come a **day or two after** the phase. For example, the highest predicted tide of 2025 was **6.34 ft on Nov. 6**, the day after the Nov. 5 full Moon. The handout's values are within about 0.2 ft of NOAA's own predictions.
- **Source:** the teacher materials name US Harbors, which republishes NOAA predictions. You can check any number at [NOAA Tides & Currents, station 8518750](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/stationhome.html?id=8518750).
:::

## 🔑 Check your graphs (try them first!)
**Daily (1/1/2025):** a smooth wave with **two highs** (5.14 ft at 9 AM; 4.00 ft at 9 PM) and **two lows** (−0.07 ft at 3 AM; −0.44 ft at 4 PM). The two highs are **not** the same height. High to high is about **12 hours**.

**Monthly (January 2025):** both lines rise and fall in waves about **two weeks apart**. AM highs peak around **5.2 ft on Jan. 1 and Jan. 12–14** (full Moon Jan. 13) and **5.3 ft on Jan. 30** (new Moon Jan. 29). They bottom out at **3.9 ft around Jan. 19–23** (third quarter Jan. 21), with a smaller dip around **Jan. 5–7** (first quarter Jan. 6). The PM line runs about 1 ft lower most of the month. The daily **range** is biggest near new and full Moon (5.8 ft on Jan. 30–31) and smallest near the quarters (3.0 ft on Jan. 22).

**Annual (2025):** two curves that move in **opposite directions**. New-moon highs peak in **April–May (6.21 ft)** and drop to **4.88 ft in December**. Full-moon highs are lowest in **March (4.91 ft)** and peak in **November (6.10 ft)** and December (5.91 ft). The peaks line up with the **shortest Moon–Earth distances** (357,136 km on Apr. 27; 356,978 km on Nov. 5). The curves cross near January and August, when new- and full-moon tides are about equal.
:::

## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
- **See:** **Daily:** two highs and two lows, a wave shape. **Monthly:** bigger and smaller highs that repeat about every **two weeks**; biggest near **new and full Moon**. **Annual:** new- and full-moon tides rise and fall over the year; biggest when the **Moon is closest**.
- **Think:** The Moon's **position** (phase) and **distance** control how high tides get. All three scales **repeat** (they're **cycles**) because the motions of the Moon and Earth repeat. The scales look alike (waves) but have different lengths.
- **Wonder:** Why two highs a day? Does the Sun matter? What happens if a storm hits on the biggest tide?

# Explain 2: Explaining Flooding in Marin County and Hurricane Sandy {#fl-explain2}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🧠 Why are some flooding events worse than others?

Your graphs showed tide patterns at three scales. Now you'll explain **why** they happen, using **gravity** and the positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon. Then you'll use that to explain why **Hurricane Sandy** and the **Marin County** floods were so severe.
:::

## Gravitational pulls on Earth {#fl-gravity}

::: {.fl-reading}
Objects in space are pulled by the **gravity** of the objects around them. The Sun's gravity keeps Earth in its orbit, and Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in orbit. The **Moon's gravity pulls on Earth too**, and it pulls the **oceans** toward it. Two **tidal bulges** form on opposite sides of Earth: **one toward the Moon**, and **one exactly opposite**.

*Why a bulge on the far side?* The Moon pulls hardest on the ocean closest to it, a bit less on Earth's center, and least on the far ocean. So the near ocean is pulled ahead of Earth, and Earth is pulled ahead of the far ocean. Both sides stretch out.
:::

Here's a model of the tidal bulges. The **Sun is on the left**, like the Monthly Tide Cycle Model in your packet. The bulges are **hugely exaggerated**. Use the three sliders for the **daily**, **monthly**, and **annual** scales.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flTideHour = Inputs.range([0, 24.8], {step: 0.1, value: 0, label: "Daily: hours since \"You\" faced the Moon:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flTideDay = Inputs.range([0, 29.5], {step: 0.1, value: 0, label: "Monthly: days since new Moon:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof flTideDist = Inputs.range([356978, 406682], {step: 1000, value: 381000, label: "Annual: Moon–Earth distance (km):"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const p = flTideDay / flSyn;
  const phiS = Math.PI, phiM = Math.PI + 2 * Math.PI * p;     // Sun to the left; new Moon toward the Sun
  const aM = Math.pow(381830 / flTideDist, 3), aS = 0.46;
  const W = 420, H = 300, cx = 230, cy = 150, re = 48, k = 15, R = 125;
  const ocean = psi => aM * Math.cos(2 * (psi - phiM)) + aS * Math.cos(2 * (psi - phiS));
  const pts = flD3.range(0, 361, 3).map(deg => {
    const psi = deg * Math.PI / 180;
    const r = re + 14 + k * ocean(psi);
    return [cx + r * Math.cos(psi), cy - r * Math.sin(psi)];
  });
  const amp = Math.hypot(aM * Math.cos(2 * phiM) + aS * Math.cos(2 * phiS), aM * Math.sin(2 * phiM) + aS * Math.sin(2 * phiS));
  const align = Math.cos(2 * (phiM - phiS));
  const kind = align > 0.7 ? "Spring tide" : align < -0.7 ? "Neap tide" : "In between";
  const near = flTideDist < 365000 ? "near perigee (close)" : flTideDist > 398000 ? "near apogee (far)" : "middle distance";
  const special = kind === "Spring tide" && flTideDist < 365000 ? "⚠️ Perigean spring tide (king tide): the most extreme tides"
                : kind === "Neap tide" && flTideDist > 398000 ? "Apogean neap tide: the least extreme tides" : "";
  const psiP = phiM + 2 * Math.PI * flTideHour / 24.84;   // "You" rotate with Earth; ~24 h 50 min to face the Moon again
  const hP = ocean(psiP);
  const youTide = hP > 0.7 * amp ? "High tide" : hP < -0.7 * amp ? "Low tide" : hP > 0 ? "Water rising or falling (above middle)" : "Water rising or falling (below middle)";
  const rP = re + 14 + k * hP;
  const px = cx + rP * Math.cos(psiP), py = cy - rP * Math.sin(psiP);
  const mx = cx + R * Math.cos(phiM), my = cy - R * Math.sin(phiM);
  const rm = 9 + 6 * (aM - 0.85);
  let s = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" role="img" aria-label="Tidal bulge model: Sun to the left, Earth in the middle with an exaggerated ocean bulge, Moon ${Math.round(flTideDay * 10) / 10} days after new Moon. ${kind}." style="width:100%;background:#0b1020;border-radius:12px;font:12px sans-serif">`;
  s += `<text x="8" y="18" fill="#fde68a" font-weight="700">☀️ Sun's pull</text>`;
  for (let j = 0; j < 6; j++) { const y = 40 + j * 46; s += `<line x1="6" y1="${y}" x2="50" y2="${y}" stroke="#fde68a" stroke-width="2" opacity=".6"/>`; }
  s += `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${R}" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/>`;
  s += `<path d="M${pts.map(q => q.join(",")).join("L")}Z" fill="#38bdf8" fill-opacity=".55" stroke="#7dd3fc"/>`;
  s += `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${re}" fill="#166534"/><text x="${cx}" y="${cy + 4}" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-weight="700">Earth</text>`;
  s += `<circle cx="${mx}" cy="${my}" r="${rm}" fill="#334155"/><path d="M${mx},${my - rm} A${rm},${rm} 0 0 0 ${mx},${my + rm}Z" fill="#f5f0d0"/>`;
  s += `<line x1="${cx}" y1="${cy}" x2="${mx}" y2="${my}" stroke="#c4b5fd" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/>`;
  s += `<circle cx="${px}" cy="${py}" r="6" fill="#f43f5e" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="${px}" y="${py - 10}" fill="#fecdd3" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">You</text>`;
  s += `</svg>`;
  const color = kind === "Spring tide" ? "#b91c1c" : kind === "Neap tide" ? "#1d4ed8" : "#475569";
  return html`<div class="fl-svg-wrap">${flSvg(s)}
  <div class="fl-cards">
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Moon phase</span><b class="fl-big">${flPhaseName(p)}</b></div>
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Tide type this week</span><b class="fl-big" style="color:${color}">${kind}</b>Moon ${near}</div>
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">At your spot ("You")</span><b class="fl-big">${youTide}</b></div>
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Bulge size (model)</span><b class="fl-big">${Math.round(amp * 100)}%</b>of the Moon's bulge alone at middle distance</div>
  </div>
  ${special ? html`<div class="fl-card" style="font-weight:700;">${special}</div>` : ""}
  <p class="fl-note">Model, not real data. The Sun's tidal pull is set to about 0.46 of the Moon's (a little under half), and the Moon's pull grows as the Moon gets closer (in proportion to 1 ÷ distance³). Real coastlines change the exact tide sizes.</p></div>`;
}
```

## Daily tidal fluctuations {#fl-daily}

As Earth spins once a day, each place on Earth is carried **through both bulges**. So places like New York get **two high tides and two low tides** a day. Because the Moon also moves along its orbit, it takes about **24 hours 50 minutes** to face the Moon again, so high tides come about **50 minutes later** each day (that's why some cells in your data table were blank!).

In class you use the **Tidal Forces Simulation** (Daily Tides tab). Try the **Daily** slider in the model above, too.

<a class="fl-sim-link" href="https://simulations.newvisions.org/tidalforces.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">🌊 Open the Tidal Forces Simulation (New Visions)</a>

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Daily Tidal Fluctuations, question 1

1. On the Daily Tide Cycle Model, draw **where a person would be** for each tide (high, low). Include **arrows** showing the gravitational pulls on Earth.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
A person **directly under the Moon** and a person on the **exact opposite side** both have **high tide** (they're on the bulges). People **90° away** (on the "sides" of Earth compared to the Moon) have **low tide**. Draw the gravity arrow from Earth's oceans **toward the Moon**. Because the Moon moves along its orbit while Earth spins, high tides come about every **12 h 25 min**, not exactly every 12 h.
:::

## Monthly tidal fluctuations {#fl-monthly}

::: {.fl-reading}
The **Sun's gravity** also pulls on Earth and its oceans. The Moon is **much closer** than the Sun, so the Moon's pull on the oceans is stronger and drives the tides. But the Sun can **strengthen or weaken** the Moon's effect, depending on whether it pulls along the **same line** or at a **right angle**. Over about **29.5 days**, the Moon orbits Earth, so the positions of the Earth, Sun, and Moon keep changing.

- When the Sun and Moon are **in a line** with Earth (new Moon and full Moon), they **add together**: the most extreme tides of the month, called **spring tides** (highest highs, lowest lows).
- When the Moon's pull and the Sun's pull are **perpendicular** (at right angles: first and third quarter), they **partly cancel**: the least extreme tides, called **neap tides**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 📌 A note about your packet's wording
The packet says "over the course of a month (**four weeks**), the moon orbits the Earth." The phase cycle that controls spring and neap tides is **29.5 days**, a bit more than four weeks. (The Moon circles Earth in about 27.3 days compared to the stars, but it takes about 2 more days to line up with the Sun again because Earth has moved along its own orbit.)

Also: **"spring" tides have nothing to do with the season.** "Spring" means the water **springs up**. They happen at **every** new and full Moon, all year.
:::

Slide the **Monthly** slider in the model above to new Moon (0), first quarter (about 7.4), full Moon (about 14.8), and third quarter (about 22.1). In class you use the **Monthly Tides** tab of the Tidal Forces Simulation.

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: questions 2–3

2. On the Monthly Tide Cycle Model (Sun on the left), **draw where the Moon is** for each moon phase. Include **arrows** for the gravitational forces on Earth, and label which phases give **stronger** tides and which give **weaker** tides.
3. Label which pictures show **spring tides** and which show **neap tides**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
Seen from above the North Pole, with the Moon orbiting counterclockwise:

- **New Moon:** Moon between Earth and the Sun (to the **left** of Earth). Sun and Moon arrows point the **same way** → **stronger** → **spring tide**.
- **First quarter:** Moon 90° around (**below** Earth on the page). Arrows at **right angles** → **weaker** → **neap tide**.
- **Full Moon:** Moon on the far side (to the **right** of Earth). Arrows point in **opposite directions along the same line**, and both stretch Earth along that line → **stronger** → **spring tide**.
- **Third quarter:** Moon **above** Earth on the page. Right angles → **weaker** → **neap tide**.

(If your drawing has the two quarters swapped, that's OK as long as your orbit direction is consistent. The key is the **90°**.)
:::

## Annual tidal fluctuations {#fl-annual}

::: {.fl-reading}
The Moon's orbit around Earth is an **ellipse** (an oval), like Earth's orbit around the Sun. So sometimes the Moon is **closer** to Earth and sometimes **farther**.

- When the Moon is closest, it's at **perigee**. Its pull on the oceans is **stronger**, so tides are more extreme.
- When the Moon is farthest, it's at **apogee**. Its pull is **weaker**, so tides are less extreme.

If the Moon is at **perigee** at the same time as a **spring tide** (new or full Moon), it's called a **perigean spring tide** (also called a **king tide**). These are the **most extreme** tides. If the Moon is at **apogee** during a **neap tide**, it's an **apogean neap tide**, the **least extreme** tides.
:::

Your packet has a graph of **Moon distance vs. tidal range in 2025**. Here it is, made from the same 24 new- and full-moon tides in your data table:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

      title: d => `${d.series.replace(" high tide", "")}, ${d.date}/2025\nDistance: ${d.dist.toLocaleString()} km\nRange: ${d.range.toFixed(2)} ft`})

})

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## 📌 A note about "annual" tides
The packet (and the unit plan) can make it sound like the Moon is closest **once a year**, like Earth's orbit. It isn't. The Moon reaches **perigee about every 27.5 days**, about once a month. What changes slowly through the year is **which phase** perigee lines up with. Perigee comes back to the **same phase** about every **14 months** (about 412 days). In 2025, that's why **new-moon** tides peaked in **March–May** and **full-moon** tides peaked in **October–December**. "Annual" is fine as a name for the time scale; just don't say "the Moon is closest once a year."
:::

### The Annual Tide Cycle Model (question 4)

This model shows Earth at four places around the Sun, each with the Moon's **oval orbit** (stretched a lot so you can see it). The **long axis of the Moon's orbit turns only slowly**, so the **perigee end (P)** points the same way in all four pictures. **A** = apogee. In class you also use the **Annual Tides** tab of the Tidal Forces Simulation.

Each Earth has an oval Moon orbit with the perigee end, P, pointing right and the apogee end, A, pointing left." style="width:100%;max-width:560px;background:#0b1020;border-radius:12px;font:12px sans-serif">`;

  spots.forEach(o => {
    s += `<ellipse cx="${o.x}" cy="${o.y}" rx="44" ry="24" fill="none" stroke="#a5b4fc" stroke-width="1.5"/>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${o.x}" cy="${o.y}" r="11" fill="#2563eb"/>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${o.x + 44}" cy="${o.y}" r="7" fill="#f5f0d0"/><text x="${o.x + 44}" y="${o.y - 11}" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fde68a" font-weight="800">P</text>`;
    s += `<text x="${o.x - 44}" y="${o.y - 8}" text-anchor="middle" fill="#cbd5e1" font-weight="800">A</text>`;
    s += `<circle cx="${o.x}" cy="${o.y + 36}" r="10" fill="#6366f1"/><text x="${o.x}" y="${o.y + 40}" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-weight="800">${o.n}</text>`;
  });
  s += `</svg>`;
  const notes = [
    "<b>1.</b> P points <b>toward</b> the Sun, so the Moon is at perigee at <b>new Moon</b>. → <b>Perigean spring tide at new Moon</b>; new-moon tides are <b>stronger</b> than full-moon tides. (Like April–May 2025.)",
    "<b>2.</b> The orbit's long axis is at a right angle to the Sun line, so perigee and apogee fall near the <b>quarter Moons</b>. → New- and full-moon tides are about the <b>same</b> strength. The quarter Moon at apogee gives an <b>apogean neap tide</b> (least extreme).",
    "<b>3.</b> P points <b>away</b> from the Sun, so the Moon is at perigee at <b>full Moon</b>. → <b>Perigean spring tide at full Moon</b>; full-moon tides are <b>stronger</b> than new-moon tides. (Like November–December 2025.)",
    "<b>4.</b> Same as 2: new- and full-moon tides about equal; <b>apogean neap tide</b> at the quarter Moon near A. (Like the crossover months, January and August 2025.)"
  ];
  return html`<div class="fl-svg-wrap">${flSvg(s)}

## Construct explanations {#fl-construct}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Construct explanations

1. How do **moon phases** affect high and low tides on a **monthly** basis? Include what a **spring tide** is and what causes it, and what a **neap tide** is and what causes it.
2. How does the **distance** of the Moon from Earth affect high and low tides on an **annual** basis? Include what **apogee** and **perigee** are, and how they affect the strength of tides.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
1. A **spring tide** is the time of the month with the **highest high tides and lowest low tides** (the biggest range). It happens at **new and full Moon**, when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are **in a line**, so the Sun's and Moon's gravity stretch the oceans along the same line and the bulges **add**. A **neap tide** has the **smallest range** (lower highs, higher lows). It happens at **first and third quarter**, when the Sun's pull is at a **right angle** to the Moon's and partly cancels it. Spring tides come about every **14–15 days**. Evidence: in January 2025 at The Battery, AM high tides were about **5.2–5.3 ft** at the spring tides vs. about **3.9 ft** at the neap tide.
2. The Moon's orbit is an **oval**. **Perigee** is its closest point and **apogee** its farthest. Closer means a **stronger pull**, so tides at perigee are **more extreme**; at apogee, **weaker**. The Moon reaches perigee about every 27.5 days, but whether that lines up with a new or full Moon changes through the year. When perigee lines up with a spring tide, tides are the most extreme of the year. Evidence: in 2025 the new-moon high tide was **6.21 ft in April** (Moon about 357,000 km away) but only **4.88 ft in December** (about 403,000 km).
:::

## Sandy and Marin County {#fl-sandy}

Now put it all together. A **storm surge** is extra water pushed toward the coast by a storm's winds (plus a small rise from low air pressure). The total water level that floods the city is the **storm tide**:

<div style="text-align:center;font-size:1.15em;font-weight:700;margin:10px 0;">storm tide = normal (predicted) tide + storm surge</div>

Below is the **real record** from The Battery during Hurricane Sandy. The **blue line** is the tide NOAA predicted from the Moon and Sun alone. The **red line** is what the water actually did. The **orange** area is the surge (red minus blue). Then try the **what-if** controls.

```{ojs}

```{ojs}

```{ojs}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const MTL = 2.47;   // mean tide level, ft above MLLW (used only to scale the what-if tides)
  const scale = flTideKind.startsWith("Neap") ? 0.67 : flTideKind.startsWith("Extra") ? 1.27 : 1;
  const tide = flPred.map(v => MTL + (v - MTL) * scale + flSLR);
  const changed = flShift !== 0 || scale !== 1 || flSLR !== 0;
  const rows = flPred.map((v, h) => {
    const j = h - flShift;
    const s = j >= 0 && j < flSurge.length ? flSurge[j] : NaN;
    return {h, tide: tide[h], surge: s, storm: tide[h] + s, obs: flObs[h]};
  }).filter(d => d.h >= 36 && d.h <= 96);
  const valid = rows.filter(d => !isNaN(d.storm));
  const peak = valid.reduce((a, b) => b.storm > a.storm ? b : a);
  const marks = [
    changed ? flPlot.lineY(rows, {x: "h", y: "obs", stroke: "#94a3b8", strokeWidth: 1.5, curve: "monotone-x"}) : null,
    flPlot.ruleY([5.05], {stroke: "#64748b", strokeDasharray: "6 4"}),
    flPlot.text([{h: 37, y: 5.05}], {x: "h", y: "y", text: () => "normal high tide (5.05 ft)", textAnchor: "start", dy: -7, fill: "currentColor", fontSize: 11}),
    flPlot.areaY(valid, {x: "h", y1: 0, y2: "surge", fill: "#f97316", fillOpacity: 0.25, curve: "monotone-x"}),
    flPlot.lineY(valid, {x: "h", y: "surge", stroke: "#ea580c", strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "3 2", curve: "monotone-x"}),
    flPlot.lineY(rows, {x: "h", y: "tide", stroke: "#0284c7", strokeWidth: 2.2, curve: "monotone-x"}),
    flPlot.lineY(valid, {x: "h", y: "storm", stroke: "#dc2626", strokeWidth: 3, curve: "monotone-x"}),
    flPlot.dot([peak], {x: "h", y: "storm", r: 6, fill: "#dc2626", stroke: "white"}),
    flPlot.text([peak], {x: "h", y: "storm", text: d => `${d.storm.toFixed(1)} ft`, dy: -14, fontWeight: 800, fill: "#dc2626"}),
    flPlot.tip(rows, flPlot.pointerX({x: "h", y: "storm", title: d => `${flHourLabel(d.h)}\nTide: ${d.tide.toFixed(1)} ft\nSurge: ${isNaN(d.surge) ? "n/a" : d.surge.toFixed(1)} ft\nStorm tide: ${isNaN(d.storm) ? "n/a" : d.storm.toFixed(1)} ft`}))
  ].filter(Boolean);
  const chart = flPlot.plot({
    title: changed ? "WHAT IF? Storm tide with your changes (gray = what really happened)" : "Hurricane Sandy at The Battery, Oct 28–30, 2012",
    subtitle: "Blue = tide · orange = storm surge · red = storm tide (water level), ft above MLLW",
    width, height: 380, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {label: null, ticks: flD3.range(36, 97, 12), tickFormat: h => flHourTick(h)},
    y: {label: "Water level (ft above MLLW)", domain: [-1, 17.5], grid: true},
    marks
  });
  return html`<div>${chart}
  <div class="fl-cards">
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Highest storm tide (this view)</span><b class="fl-big">${peak.storm.toFixed(1)} ft</b>${flHourLabel(peak.h)} (hourly data)</div>
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Real peak (6-minute data)</span><b class="fl-big">14.06 ft</b>Oct 29, 9:24 pm EDT</div>
    <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Change from what really happened</span><b class="fl-big">${changed ? (peak.storm - 13.99 >= 0 ? "+" : "") + (peak.storm - 13.99).toFixed(1) + " ft" : "0 ft"}</b>vs. hourly peak 13.99 ft</div>
  </div></div>`;
}
```

<p class="fl-note">Data: NOAA CO-OPS station 8518750 (The Battery, NY), hourly verified water level and tide predictions, ft above MLLW, EDT. Surge = observed − predicted. The "what if" options are a <b>simple model</b>, not real events: the surge curve is shifted in time, the tide is stretched or shrunk around mean tide level (neap-size ≈ an Oct. 2012 neap tide; extra-large ≈ the Oct. 16, 2012 spring tide), and sea-level rise is added to every hour.</p>

- Move the surge **6 hours** later (to low tide). How much lower is the peak?

## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
**Alignment + a close Moon = the biggest tides.** Sandy hit on a **full-Moon spring tide**, so the water was already higher than normal when the surge arrived. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)
Coastal flood height = the **tide** + the **storm surge**. Tides are set by the positions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon. Sandy reached New York on **Oct. 29, 2012, a full Moon**, so it was a **spring tide**: the Sun and Moon pulled along one line and high tide was higher than normal. Sandy's winds pushed a surge of about **9.3 ft** into the harbor near the **evening high tide**, so the water at The Battery reached a record **14.06 ft above MLLW**, about **9 ft above a normal high tide**, flooding subways and tunnels. In Marin County, the flooding came during a **perigean spring tide** (king tide): alignment **plus** a close Moon made the most extreme tides, so water topped the shoreline even with little storm push. **Same kind of storm, different tide timing = very different damage.**
:::

::: {.key-idea}
### 🔑 Class consensus: tides and extreme flooding
- **Daily:** high tide happens where the ocean faces **toward or away from** the Moon.
- **Monthly:** **spring tides** (most extreme) at new and full Moon, when the Sun and Moon pull **along the same line**; **neap tides** (least extreme) when they pull at **right angles**.
- **Annual:** tides are more extreme when the Moon is at **perigee** than at **apogee**. The biggest ranges are **perigean spring tides**.
- **Sandy** struck on a **spring tide**, so when storm winds blew water onto land, there was more water ready to flood. **Marin** flooded on a **perigean spring tide**.
- **Lingering question:** the Moon's cycles haven't changed in thousands of years. **So why is coastal flooding getting worse?**
:::

The **annual** scale showed that some spring tides are much bigger than others, matching when the Moon was **closest**. Together: alignment (monthly) **plus** a close Moon (changing over the year) = **perigean spring tides**, the most extreme tides.
- **Observer:** From Earth we see **phases** because of our viewing angle; an observer at the Sun or far outside the system would not. Tides depend on **where you are** too: a place facing toward or away from the Moon has high tide while a place 90° away has low tide, so different coasts get high tide at different times. Everyone sees the **same phase** on the same day, but the **local tide** depends on where you stand (and on the shape of the coast).
:::

# Elaborate: Designing Solutions for Worsening Floods {#fl-elaborate}

::: {.elaborate-box}
## 🛠️ How do engineers design local solutions to global problems?

The Moon explains why **some** floods are worse than others. But the Moon's cycles repeat the same way year after year. So why is coastal flooding happening **more often**? In this phase you'll find out, and then you'll **design your own solution** with your group.
:::

## Part 1: Read-Generate-Sort-Solve {#fl-rgss}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Read-Generate-Sort-Solve

**Prompt:** How has the **frequency of high-tide flooding** changed over the past **50 years**? **Why** has that change happened, and how is it predicted to affect flooding in the **future**?

1. **Read** the article *Climate Change: Global Sea Level* (NOAA Climate.gov).
2. **Generate** ideas with your group on chart paper.
3. **Sort:** discuss each idea and ☆ **star** the most useful ones.
4. **Solve:** on your own, write your response to the prompt using the starred ideas.
:::

<a class="fl-sim-link" href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level" target="_blank" rel="noopener">📰 Read: Climate Change: Global Sea Level (NOAA Climate.gov)</a>

Key numbers to look for as you read:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-cards">
  <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Global sea level since 1880</span><b class="fl-big">+8 to 9 in</b>(21–24 cm)</div>
  <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">Speed of the rise</span><b class="fl-big">0.06 → 0.14 in/yr</b>20th century → 2006–2015: more than doubled</div>
  <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">U.S. high-tide flooding</span><b class="fl-big">300% to 900%+</b>more frequent than 50 years ago</div>
  <div class="fl-stat"><span class="fl-lab">The Battery, NYC (NOAA tide gauge)</span><b class="fl-big">1.16 in per decade</b>sea-level trend, 1856–2025 (about 1 ft per century)</div>
</div>
```

<p class="fl-note">Sources: NOAA Climate.gov, <i>Climate Change: Global Sea Level</i>; NOAA Tides &amp; Currents Sea Level Trends, station 8518750.</p>

**Why this matters for tides:** every high tide now starts from a **higher sea**. A spring tide or king tide that used to stay below the street can now reach it, even on a **sunny day** with no storm. And every storm surge starts from higher water too. (Try the sea-level slider in the [Sandy model](#fl-sandy).)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Solve (try it first!)
High-tide flooding in the U.S. is now **300% to more than 900% more frequent** than 50 years ago. The cause is **sea-level rise**: global sea level is up **8–9 inches since 1880**, and the rate **more than doubled** (from 0.06 in/yr in the 1900s to 0.14 in/yr in 2006–2015) as warming **melts glaciers and ice sheets** and **warms (expands) ocean water**. Higher seas mean ordinary spring tides and king tides now reach streets. Sea level is likely to rise **at least 1 more foot** above 2000 levels by 2100 even if emissions are low, so flooding will become **more frequent**, and storm surges will start from **higher water**. (Numbers: NOAA Climate.gov.)
:::

## Part 2: Designing Solutions {#fl-design}

Climate change is a **global** problem with far-reaching impacts. Like any big problem, it can be **broken down into smaller problems** that engineering can solve. First, practice telling **criteria** from **constraints**:

- **Criteria** = what a solution **must do** to succeed (its requirements).
- **Constraints** = the **limits** it has to work within (money, space, time, materials, rules).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
flSorter(["Criterion", "Constraint"], [
  {text: "It must keep out a storm tide as high as Sandy's.", cat: "Criterion", why: "That's what the design has to do."},
  {text: "It must fit in the narrow space between the river and existing buildings and subways.", cat: "Constraint", why: "Space is a limit the design must work within."},
  {text: "The city's budget for the project is limited.", cat: "Constraint", why: "Money is a limit."},
  {text: "It should protect subway entrances.", cat: "Criterion", why: "Protecting subways is a goal the design must meet."},
  {text: "It can't block ships, storm drains, or sewers.", cat: "Constraint", why: "A rule or limit the design has to respect."},
  {text: "It should keep working for at least 50 years as sea level rises.", cat: "Criterion", why: "A performance goal: something it must do."}
], "Now write criteria and constraints for your own problem.")
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Part 2. Designing Solutions

Describe **one way climate change is showing up in a local community**. Then:

1. List at least **3 criteria** for a successful solution.
2. **Prioritize** your top three criteria in order of importance.
3. Name at least **3 constraints** the solution has to work within.
4. With your group, **brainstorm** solutions.
5. As a group, choose one solution and **design** it: include a **drawing** and a description of how it works.
6. Describe the **costs and benefits** of your design.

In class, groups post their designs for an **Idea Carousel**: you rotate and leave sticky notes on other groups' posters (a strength, a constraint they missed, a question), then revise your own.
:::

Draft your group's design here (saved in this browser only):

```{ojs}

flForm("flDesign-flooding", "Designing Solutions for Worsening Floods", [
  ["local", "A local problem: how is climate change showing up in a community near you?"],
  ["q1", "1. At least 3 criteria for a successful solution"],
  ["q2", "2. My top three criteria, most important first"],
  ["q3", "3. At least 3 constraints"],
  ["q4", "4. Brainstorm: possible solutions"],
  ["q5", "5. Our design: how it works (sketch it on paper too)"],
  ["q6c", "6. Costs"],
  ["q6b", "6. Benefits"]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Sample design (many answers can be right)
- **Local problem:** high tides plus storm surge flood streets, basements, and subway entrances in low parts of NYC (lower Manhattan, Red Hook, the Rockaways) more and more often as sea level rises.
- **Criteria (prioritized):** 1. Keep water out of homes and subways during a storm tide at least as high as Sandy's (14 ft above MLLW at The Battery) **plus** future sea-level rise. 2. Protect the people least able to recover. 3. Keep the waterfront usable every day. (Others: lasts for decades; low upkeep.)
- **Constraints:** budget; limited space between the water and buildings; can't block shipping, drains, or sewers; construction time; community approval; can't push the flooding onto neighbors.
- **Brainstorm:** raised parks and berms, deployable flood gates, raising streets and bulkheads, wetlands and oyster reefs that slow waves, raising buildings and equipment, pumps, buyouts of the most-flooded homes.
- **Design idea:** a raised waterfront park with a **berm**, plus **flood gates** at subway entrances that are closed using **tide predictions** (for example, before perigean spring tides and forecast surges).
- **Benefits:** fewer flooded homes and stations, lower repair costs, safer evacuation, a park for daily use. **Costs:** construction money, lost views or access, upkeep, water redirected toward unprotected neighbors, habitat loss (walls) or slower protection (wetlands).
:::

# Evaluate: Revisiting the Performance Task: Flooding {#fl-evaluate}

::: {.evaluate-box}
## 🔗 How can we design solutions aimed at the problem of storm damage?

**Engineering component: design elements.** A solution can be broken into **design elements**: parts you would **change, add, or take away** from the system to address the problem. A design element's ability to address the problem is its **benefit**. It may also have unintended consequences, or **costs**. When evaluating a solution, you weigh benefits against costs to decide if the **tradeoff** is worth it.

This page is in your **Performance Task Organizer (PTO)**, not your Flooding packet. It's evidence for your **Final Performance Task**.
:::

  ["q1", "1. Explain what caused the flooding in either Hurricane Sandy or Marin County."],
  ["q2", "2. Why is this a problem that we need to address?"],
  ["q3", "3. Design a solution to address the problem. Describe it (and sketch it on paper)."],
  ["q4c", "4. Costs of your solution design"],
  ["q4b", "4. Benefits of your solution design"],
  ["q5", "5. Describe the constraints or limitations of the solution."],
  ["q6", "6. Design element(s) in the system, and how each addresses the problem and connects to the science"]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Sample proficient answers (try yours first!)
1. **Sandy:** On Oct. 29, 2012 the Moon was **full**, so the Sun, Earth, and Moon were nearly **in line** and their pulls added: a **spring tide**. Sandy's winds and low pressure pushed a **storm surge** of about **9.3 ft** into New York Harbor, arriving near the **evening high tide**. Storm tide = tide + surge, so the water at The Battery hit a record **14.06 ft above MLLW**, about 9 ft above a normal high tide. (**Marin:** a **perigean spring tide**, a new or full Moon with the Moon near perigee, made extreme high tides, and storm water on top pushed the bay over roads and into homes.) **Sea-level rise** means every tide now starts higher than in the past.
2. Coastal floods damage homes, subways, and power, and harm people, especially those who can't evacuate or afford repairs. The flooding is **predictable** (tides) and getting **more frequent** with sea-level rise, so the damage will grow unless we plan.
3. A **raised waterfront park with a berm**, plus **deployable gates** at subway entrances closed using NOAA tide and surge forecasts, **raised electrical equipment**, and a **wetland edge**.
4. **Costs:** high construction cost, years to build, gates must be staffed and maintained, may send water toward unprotected neighbors, temporary loss of park access. **Benefits:** blocks storm tides like Sandy's, protects transit and homes, a park for daily use, wetlands absorb wave energy.
5. Limited space and budget; must allow drainage and shipping; needs community approval; sea level keeps rising, so the height must allow for the future; a surge bigger than the design height will still flood.
6. **Berm built higher than Sandy's storm tide + 1 ft:** storm tide = tide + surge, so the height is set by the worst case (spring tide + surge) plus sea-level rise. **Gates closed on tide forecasts:** tides are predictable from Sun-Moon positions, so close them before perigean spring tides and forecast surges. **Wetland edge:** slows waves and absorbs some surge before it reaches the berm.

**Most common gap:** "Sandy flooded because of the full Moon." For Proficient, explain **how** the Sun-Moon alignment raised the tide, and that the storm surge **added on top**.
:::

# Chapter Summary {#fl-chapter-summary}

::: {.fl-table-wrap}
| Key concept | What to remember |
|---|---|
| **Moon phases** | The Sun always lights **half** the Moon. The phase is how much of that lit half we see from Earth, set by the Moon's **position in its orbit**. Not Earth's shadow. |
| **Lunar cycle** | New → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → third quarter → waning crescent → new, every **29.5 days**. |
| **Eclipses** | **Solar** = new Moon in an exact line (Moon's shadow on Earth; seen in a narrow path). **Lunar** = full Moon in an exact line (Earth's shadow on the Moon; seen from the whole night side). Rare because the Moon's orbit is **tilted about 5°**. |
| **Daily tides** | The Moon's gravity makes **two bulges**; Earth spins through both → **two highs and two lows** a day, about 50 min later each day. |
| **Spring tides** | New and full Moon; Sun and Moon pull **along the same line** → biggest range. About every 14–15 days. |
| **Neap tides** | Quarter Moons; pulls at **right angles** → smallest range. |
| **Perigee / apogee** | The Moon's **closest / farthest** point. Closer = stronger tides. **Perigean spring tide (king tide)** = the most extreme tides. |
| **The Battery data** | Jan. 2025: spring high tides about 5.2–5.3 ft vs. neap about 3.9 ft. 2025: new-moon high 6.21 ft (April, ~357,000 km) vs. 4.88 ft (December, ~403,000 km). |
| **Storm tide** | Storm tide = tide + storm surge. Sandy: ~9.3 ft surge near high tide on a full-Moon spring tide → record **14.06 ft above MLLW**. |
| **Sea-level rise** | +8–9 in globally since 1880, rising faster now; high-tide flooding 300–900%+ more frequent than 50 years ago. Every tide and surge starts higher. |
| **Design** | Criteria (what it must do), constraints (limits), design elements (parts you add, change, or remove), costs vs. benefits (tradeoffs). |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 📚 Data and sources in this chapter
- **Tides at The Battery, NY:** class handout *Tidal Fluctuation Data* (NOAA predictions via US Harbors); NOAA CO-OPS Tides & Currents, station 8518750 (predictions, verified water levels, datums: MHHW 5.05 ft above MLLW).
- **Hurricane Sandy:** NOAA CO-OPS hourly verified water level and predictions, Oct. 27–31, 2012; record 14.06 ft above MLLW at 9:24 pm EDT, Oct. 29, 2012 (6-minute data).
- **Winter Storm Jonas:** NOAA CO-OPS, 7.43 ft above MLLW at 8:00 am, Jan. 23, 2016 (predicted 5.09 ft).
- **Moon facts:** NASA Moon Fact Sheet (29.53-day phase cycle, 27.32-day orbit compared to the stars, ~5.1° tilt). Moon phase dates and the moon calendar are **calculated**.
- **Sea level:** NOAA Climate.gov, *Climate Change: Global Sea Level*; NOAA Tides & Currents Sea Level Trends (The Battery, 1.16 in per decade, 1856–2025).
- **Models in this chapter** (labeled where they appear): the virtual ball-and-flashlight model, the eclipse side view, the tidal bulge model, the Annual Tide Cycle Model, and the Sandy "what-if" options.
- **Simulators:** UNL Moon Phases Simulator and Eclipse Explorer; New Visions Tidal Forces Simulation.
- **Packet corrections noted in this chapter:** the phase cycle is 29.5 days (not 28 or "four weeks"); the Moon's tilt stays ~5° (it doesn't "become aligned"); the missing moon calendar; the blank Moon Phase column in the January data; perigee happens about monthly, not once a year; who can see a lunar eclipse and when the new Moon is up.
:::

  const scoreEl = header.querySelector(".fl-score");
  flBuildCards(body, questions, ok => { nDone++; if (ok) nRight++; scoreEl.textContent = `Score: ${nRight} / ${nDone}`; });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```
